output.title: Rubber-stamped approval has a hidden workflow cost
output.body:
If you run a small business, the quiet cost of rubber-stamped approval usually shows up in one place: a recurring decision you approve because it is faster than checking it properly. That can be invoice sign-off, a refund, a data entry check, or a customer request that gets passed through on habit.

The cost is not dramatic. It is the extra minute of doubt before you click yes. It is the second look later when the same item lands back on your desk. In a small business, that kind of friction adds up because the owner often becomes the default approval layer.

The useful question is not whether every approval should be automated. It is whether the approval rule is clear enough to be enforced. If the rule is simple, a bounded automation step can flag exceptions and leave the decision with you. If the rule is fuzzy, software just turns confusion into faster confusion. Helpful, in a very specific way.

For a practical next step, map one recurring approval flow and mark exactly where human sign-off must stay in place. Then ask: what rule would catch most bad cases before I approve them?
